title: Fair Recruitment and Selection Through Relevant Evidence
before: A conversation about connecting hiring decisions to the capabilities the work requires and the evidence applicants actually show.

turns.text: This course is Fair Recruitment and Selection Through Relevant Evidence. It’s mainly for supervisors and anyone who serves on a hiring panel or reviews an opportunity. The idea running through it is that fairer decisions rest on relevant evidence. That means telling apart what a job truly requires from credentials or preferences that just feel familiar.

The opening case is a practice panel note that says, this candidate felt like a good fit. Most of us have heard that, or written it. The course asks what evidence about the work is missing. A favorable impression might be worth exploring, but it can’t replace a criterion. You start with the capability the position needs.

The course gives three linked terms. A capability is something the work requires. A criterion explains how it will be assessed. Evidence is what the applicant actually demonstrates. Keeping those links visible is the core of the course. An impressive title, a familiar background, or confident delivery doesn’t automatically establish the capability.

The first practice situation is about a service advisory opportunity that seeks knowledge of access barriers but only recognizes formal job titles, so people with real, relevant experience may be left out. You’ll decide what should be examined. It connects to a broader point: describe the work before you describe the ideal person, and separate requirements from preferences that resemble the current team.

Then the course looks at the interview itself. A question about a relevant example can reveal actions, judgment, and results, while a vague request to describe fit may mostly reveal self-presentation. On access, a change in format or an approved support arrangement may let the same skill be shown. The proper process handles accommodations; a course can’t approve an exception.

The second situation is one that can happen quietly. A panel likes a familiar applicant and starts valuing confidence over the approved evidence of analytical reasoning. You’ll choose how to respond. The course points out that a standard which moves after an answer can advantage familiarity, even when each decision is described as professional judgment.

That ties into deliberation. A strong first opinion can shape what others remember. When ratings differ, look at the source of the difference in the notes. Seniority, agreement, or a confident statement isn’t a substitute for the actual answer. And probing should be consistent, so familiarity doesn’t decide who gets extra help or which gaps get overlooked.

The third situation involves a panel member who’s asked to give the view of an entire community because of their identity. You’ll consider a more appropriate approach. Community experience can deepen a panel’s understanding of the work, but no panelist or applicant should be expected to represent a whole group. Expertise gets assessed through criteria, not inferred from identity.

The course is also honest about what patterns can and can’t tell us. Outreach, criteria, access, probing, and deliberation interact across many selections. A selection difference alone can’t establish the cause, but it can prompt a closer look at the process. And later job success doesn’t by itself prove that the route into the job was fair.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite a practice note that says, the candidate is polished and fits our culture. The task is to name the actual capability, the evidence needed, and what the answer does or doesn’t establish. You won’t invent a criterion or replace a real hiring procedure. Those decisions stay with the responsible hiring process.

As you go, think of a hiring panel, a posting, or an opportunity you’ve been part of. Where did a criterion stay connected to the work, and where might an impression have taken its place? Bring that situation with you. Comparing for the work is something every panelist can practice, one note at a time.

guidance.title: Keeping the links visible
guidance.text: Try reading a panel note and asking which capability it refers to, which criterion applies, and what the applicant actually said or did. If you can’t trace all three, the note may be recording an impression. That doesn’t make the impression wrong, but it means it isn’t yet evidence. Writing the link down helps the whole panel compare the same things.

guidance.title: From selection into the first months
guidance.text: Think about a recent selection you were part of or saw. Did the expectations used to choose someone carry into onboarding and early feedback, or did a broader sense of fit take over? Where could clear criteria and workable access continue into the person’s first months? Who on your team would need to be part of that conversation?
